cycle and ultimately an elevated ammonia level. During adult-
hood, protein needs are decreased, because there is less need
for growth and a decreased rate of tissue turnover. Th e protein-
restricted diets prescribed need to be maintained throughout

For patients with the more severe variants of the disorder, 
some of the natural protein that is provided from foods, which 
includes a mixture of essential and nonessential amino ac-
ids, may be replaced with an essential amino acid mixture to 
ensure that the individual receives a suﬃ  cient amount of these
proteins. When one of these mixtures is ingested, the body’s
surplus nitrogen is used to synthesize the nonessential amino 
acids, thereby reducing the load on the urea cycle. In general, 
it is suggested that about 25% to 50% of total protein intake be
provided as essential amino acids. Th ere are special metabolic 
formulas designed for treatment of urea cycle disorders that
